content: 1. The management of hypertension in adults involves significant variability in patient and provider perspectives. While society and patients generally aim to reduce the risk of premature mortality and morbidity, there is limited data on whether patients prefer blood pressure (BP) management by physicians versus other healthcare providers. Some patients appreciate self-care applications, while others express concerns about the potential harm to the patient-doctor relationship, particularly with the use of home-monitoring devices. 2. In-depth interviews with UK patients revealed concerns about clinical governance, privacy, and space availability in community pharmacies for nurse and pharmacist prescribing. However, patients were less concerned about nursing management. A study in Scotland showed high patient satisfaction with pharmacist prescribing, but 65% of patients preferred consulting a doctor. 3. Task shifting in the public sector may reduce health inequities by increasing access to underserved areas. Community team approaches for hypertension management are estimated to cost around USD 200 per person per year, with potential cost savings from cardiovascular disease prevention, resulting in a median net cost of USD 65 per person per year. Pharmacist-led programs are generally more cost-effective than nurse-led ones. 4. The cost-effectiveness of team-based interventions varies across economic settings, with most estimates well below USD 50,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). For middle-income countries, even a cost of USD 1,000 per QALY is acceptable, though this may not apply to low-income countries. Programs led by nurses or pharmacists may offer cost savings compared to physician-led programs. 5. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) proposed four conditions for non-physician prescribing of antihypertensives: proper training, prescribing authority, adherence to management protocols, and physician oversight. Community health workers (HCWs) can assist with education, medication delivery, BP measurement, and monitoring within a collaborative care model. Telemonitoring and community-based self-care are tools to enhance BP control. 6. Hypertension is prevalent in disaster and humanitarian settings, such as wars, earthquakes, and refugee crises. These situations disrupt healthcare systems, leading to treatment interruptions and increased cardiac morbidity and mortality. Post-traumatic stress disorder and severe injury are independent risk factors for hypertension in these populations. 7. There is limited data on hypertension control, care access, and treatment in crisis-affected populations, particularly in Africa and Asia. Agencies providing emergency care should prioritize hypertension assessment and resource allocation to prevent significant mortality and morbidity. 8. Hypertension increases the risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes, including ICU admission and mortality. Initial reports showed higher hypertension rates among severely ill COVID-19 patients, but it remains unclear if this relationship is causal or confounded by other comorbidities like obesity and diabetes. 9. Concerns about the use of ACE inhibitors (ACEis) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) in COVID-19 patients arose due to their interaction with ACE2, the receptor for SARS-CoV-2. However, observational studies found no association between ACEi/ARB use and increased COVID-19 severity. Discontinuing these medications in high-risk patients may lead to worse outcomes. 10. Most professional societies recommend continuing ACEis/ARBs in COVID-19-infected patients. Further research is needed to clarify the role of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) in COVID-19 pathogenesis and treatment. 11. Hypertension in pregnancy, including chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia, and eclampsia, is a common medical condition with significant maternal and fetal consequences. Up to 10% of pregnancy-related deaths are attributed to hypertension, and its prevalence is increasing. 12. Hypertension in pregnancy is diagnosed when BP is ≥140/90 mmHg on at least two occasions, six hours apart. Chronic hypertension is diagnosed before 20 weeks of gestation, while gestational hypertension is diagnosed at 20 weeks or later. Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia require immediate medical management. 13. Pharmacologic treatment for hypertension in pregnancy is generally initiated when systolic BP is ≥160 mmHg and/or diastolic BP is ≥105 mmHg. Preferred medications include methyldopa, beta-blockers (e.g., labetalol), calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine), and direct-acting vasodilators (e.g., hydralazine). 14. Certain antihypertensive medications, such as ACEis, ARBs, and spironolactone, are contraindicated in pregnancy due to adverse fetal effects. Atenolol is also contraindicated due to its association with intrauterine growth restriction. 15. Medication selection during pregnancy is based on long-term clinical use and experience, as most drugs are not specifically studied for efficacy and safety in pregnancy. Beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are more effective than methyldopa in preventing severe hypertension later in pregnancy. 16. The management of hypertension in pregnancy requires careful consideration of maternal and fetal risks, with treatment tailored to individual patient needs. Further research is needed to optimize treatment approaches and improve outcomes for hypertensive disorders in pregnancy.
